assumptions: Plaid is approved at production.plaid.com only; sandbox is not in the workspace
Approved vendors are exactly the hosts the customer named, Stripe and Plaid, with no LLM, email or cloud providers approved
The customer wants cardholder name and expiry not stored at all, per 'cardholder stuff can't be stored raw'
Bank account and routing numbers are in scope of 'bank data' for marking sensitive, not for forbidding
Advisory enforcement is right for a first set of policies; the customer decides whether to make them blocking
No application code should change in this pass, since fixing the findings changes stored data and behaviour

confusions: The recipe for protect_card_data suggests a charge_card function and a sensitive attribute on card_last4 and billing_address. The workspace has no billing_address field, and the recipe does not say what to do when the existing charge flow stores raw card data. I had to decide that myself: no build, findings predicted.

The card-field rule uses exact names. The recipe example lists cvv, but this workspace names the column card_cvv, so the template would silently miss it. I only caught it on re-reading my own file. The recipe should warn that field names must match the schema exactly, or list both spellings.
VND-001 with providers left empty: the catalogue says empty providers reports all as not yet reviewed, but it is unclear whether that applies to every kind or only agent.llm. I assumed every kind.
outbound.vendor_allowlist has no data-flow scope. Table scope does not catch an api.request that carries card data without touching a table, so the fraud-check endpoint is only covered by its host.

DATA-010's limits say it judges what each statement fetches, but the skill's recipe reads like it judges the response. The skill's 'No check reads an object's response' is clearer, and I relied on it.
It is not clear whether policy-level tags (pci-dss) mean anything to a check or only to filtering. I used them for labelling only.
The skill says a template fits 'when its title, rules or words cover the request'. Several templates cover card data only in part, so the choice of which to include was a judgement call, not a rule.
wished_for: A PCI DSS recipe that lists exact field names to check against a sample schema, with a note that names must match, not just resemble
A way to scope outbound.vendor_allowlist to the objects that carry a given field or param (for example card_number in an api.request params), not just to hosts
A check or param that reads the response, or at least the fields a db.add returns
A worked example of a multi-key policy mixing template rules with extra rules, so the key choice for the extra rules is clearer
Guidance on whether 'cardholder data' means PCI's definition or the customer's wording, since the two differ on name and expiry
why_confidence: The policies parse, the dry run is clean, and each stated rule maps to a check that reads the matching part of the ask. Confidence is only medium because (a) I did not run evaluate, so the predicted findings are unverified; (b) the response leak and the content of vendor payloads are invisible to the checks; and (c) the policies will not pass on the current code, which stores raw card data and logs input. A PCI audit would also need controls outside definitions. I also caught and fixed one exact-name miss (card_cvv) in my own rule while checking predictions, so an unchecked gap of the same kind may remain.
